import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 699

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/699](https://www.erdosproblems.com/699)
-/

namespace Erdos699

/-- Sylvester and Schur: for $1 \le i \le n/2$ there is a prime $p > i$ dividing `n.choose i`. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/AllenGrahamHart/FormalConjectures-Bench/blob/482dacc4d9335240f26218cdc62032da3100392b/formalizations/erdos699/Erdos699Formalization.lean#L7679"]
theorem sylvester_schur (n i : ℕ) (hi : 1 ≤ i) (hi_half : i ≤ n / 2) :
    ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ i < p ∧ p ∣ Nat.choose n i := by
  sorry

/--
**Erdős Problem 699.** Is it true that for every $1 \le i < j \le n / 2$ there exists a prime
$p \ge i$ with $p \mid \gcd\big(\binom{n}{i}, \binom{n}{j}\big)$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_699 : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ n i j : ℕ,
      1 ≤ i →
      i < j →
      j ≤ n / 2 →
      ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ i ≤ p ∧ p ∣ Nat.gcd (Nat.choose n i) (Nat.choose n j) := by
  sorry

/-- Erdős and Szekeres conjectured that, apart from a finite exceptional set of triples `(n, i, j)`,
one can always take `p > i` in the prime divisor statement. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_szekeres_strengthening : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ E : Finset (ℕ × ℕ × ℕ), ∀ n i j : ℕ,
      1 ≤ i →
      i < j →
      j ≤ n / 2 →
      (n, i, j) ∉ E →
      ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ i < p ∧ p ∣ Nat.gcd (Nat.choose n i) (Nat.choose n j) := by
  sorry

end Erdos699

findings.description: The single `∃ E : Finset (ℕ × ℕ × ℕ)` preceding all three universal quantifiers asserts global finiteness of the exceptional triples, including those with i = 2 or 3. In fact, its RHS is equivalent to the existence of a uniform N such that the strict prime-divisor conclusion holds for every admissible triple with n > N; this equivalence was proved in the scratch file. The source's wording, 'except in a few special cases', discusses low-index exceptional regimes separately and does not explicitly assert their global finiteness. Thus the Lean statement and its docstring commit to a potentially stronger interpretation that needs confirmation. This is not a demonstrated counterexample to the Lean statement: the sources consulted do not establish infinitely many exceptional triples.
findings.source_evidence: Erdős and Szekeres, 'Some number theoretic problems on binomial coefficients', Austral. Math. Soc. Gaz. 5 (1978), pp. 97–98, equation (5), https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1978-46.pdf: the strict inequality 'holds except in a few special cases'. They discuss i = 2 with n = 2^r = pq + 1 and suitable j, then scattered counterexamples for i = 3, and specifically say, 'For i ≥ 4 there should only be a few incidental counterexamples'. https://www.erdosproblems.com/699 repeats the 'few special cases' wording and the separate low-index discussion.
findings.suggested_fix: Clarify the intended scope of the exceptions against a precise reference. If the intended variant concerns finitely many incidental exceptions for i ≥ 4, replace `1 ≤ i` with `4 ≤ i` and identify that restricted variant in the docstring. Retaining all i requires either an explicit description of the exceptional low-index regimes or a reference that actually conjectures global finiteness.

https://math.berkeley.edu/~gbergman/papers/ and https://math.berkeley.edu/~gbergman/papers/nomial.tex — Bergman's On common divisors of multinomial coefficients, introduction, relevant bounds, and references.

could_not_verify: Erdos699.erdos_szekeres_strengthening: the original wording does not settle whether 'few special cases' means a globally finite set of triples or exceptional parameter regimes. The questionable finding records this unresolved interpretation, not an established false conjecture.
review.notes: Sylvester–Schur and the main question faithfully match the source. The external proof has exactly the stated Sylvester–Schur hypotheses and conclusion. The website still records problem 699 as open; its newer results cover only subranges. Lean checks verified the natural-division bound against rational n/2, gcd divisibility against simultaneous divisibility, and positivity of both binomial coefficients under the hypotheses. Computation through n = 100 found no failures of the main claim and strict failures only at (10,3,5), (16,2,6), (28,3,14), and (28,5,14); these finite examples do not refute the finite-exception statement. Scratch files in /workspace/review compile without errors or proof holes. No repository files were edited.
